sections.overview: The brown bear ranges widely across Eurasia and North America, from forests and mountains to tundra and coasts. Separated populations differ in size, coat, seasonal routines, and food choices according to local conditions. In North America, the grizzly is a brown bear subspecies within this same species.
sections.identification: Adults have a heavy body, muscular shoulder hump, and long foreclaws for digging. Their coat ranges from blond or pale brown to dark brown or black; pale tips on guard hairs can look grizzled. They walk plantigrade, with the whole foot on the ground. Adults are about 1.5–2.1 m long and 0.9–1.5 m at the shoulder; reported masses span roughly 90–450 kg depending on sex, region and season, with males generally larger.
sections.habitat: The species occupies forests, shrublands, grasslands, wetlands, and other terrestrial habitats. In Alaska, bears use low slopes and wetlands for spring greens, berry openings in summer, then salmon rivers or alpine berry patches in autumn. Seasonal movements follow food.
sections.diet: Brown bears are omnivores, eating grasses, roots, berries, nuts, fish, insects, small mammals, carrion, and sometimes larger prey. Yellowstone examples include trout, elk calves, roots, berries, and pine seeds; coastal Alaskan bears can exploit salmon runs.
sections.behavior: In Yellowstone, grizzlies are usually solitary outside courtship, family groups, or concentrated foods; some gather at streams, carcasses, or moth aggregations. They den through winter, though timing and emergence vary with sex and reproductive status.
sections.reproduction: In Yellowstone, mating is from mid-May to mid-July. After delayed implantation, cubs are born in dens in late January or February, usually one to three per litter, occasionally four. They nurse through winter and generally stay with their mother about two years.
sections.ecology: In Alaska, seasonal movements bring bears to salmon streams and berry patches in turn; accumulated fat helps support winter denning. These rich feeding sites may attract many bears to one place, particularly where food is abundant.
sections.conservation: The IUCN SSC Bear Specialist Group reports the species has been globally Least Concern since 1996 and is stable overall. This masks threatened isolated populations and past range losses. A 2023 European update reported recovery and expansion in several large populations.
